title: Not Sleeping This Winter
summary: Bruno decides that this year he won't hibernate, because he wants to see the snow with his own eyes.

scenes.text:
Autumn came to the forest smelling of damp earth and apples.

The trees turned yellow and red, and the path filled up with dry leaves.

In every cave and burrow, everyone was in a hurry. The marmots carried seeds. The dormice made beds of moss. The tortoises looked for the softest mud by the stream.

"Off to bed, off to bed, winter's coming!" they told each other, yawning.

And in the middle of all that yawning was Bruno, a brown bear with round ears and a big tummy.

Bruno wasn't yawning. Bruno was stepping on leaves, one by one, just to hear them rustle.

And there was an idea going round and round in his head.

"I'm not going to hibernate this year," Bruno announced that night.

His grandma, Rosalinda the bear, stopped knitting and looked at him over her glasses.

"What do you mean, you're not? Bears sleep all winter. It's what we do."

"That's just it," said Bruno. "Everyone tells me what winter's like, and no bear has ever seen it. They say the sky turns white. That water goes hard. I want to see it!"

Grandma thought for a long time. Then she carried on knitting.

She knitted all night. And the next morning, she hung a scarf around Bruno's neck, with stripes of every colour.

"For the cold," she said. "Eat lots. And if you get sleepy, come home."

The first days of winter were a party.

The forest went so quiet that Bruno could hear his own footsteps on the frost.

The puddles on the path had gone as hard as plates. Bruno stepped on one very carefully, and it went: crick!

It made him laugh so much that he stepped on all of them.

He discovered things no bear had ever seen. The steam that came out of his mouth, like smoke from a kettle. Spider webs turned into crystal necklaces. The last blackberries, frozen, tasting like forest sorbet.

At night he went back to the cave and told Grandma all about it. She was asleep, curled up in a ball at the very back.

Grandma answered him by snoring.

One morning, Bruno woke up because the silence sounded different.

He went out of the cave and stood there with his mouth open.

Thousands of little white dots were falling from the sky, twirling slowly, in no hurry at all. They landed on his nose, on his ears, on his scarf. They didn't make any noise. Just a cold little tickle, as if the air were full of feathers.

It was snow.

Bruno stuck out his tongue and caught a flake. It tasted of nothing, and of cold, and of something new.

He flopped onto his back and waved his arms and legs. When he got up, there was a picture in the snow: a bear with wings.

"It was worth it," Bruno said, very quietly. "It was worth staying awake."

The next day, the forest lake wasn't water any more. It was a mirror.

Bruno put one paw on it, very, very carefully. Then another. Then all four.

And then he slipped, and landed on his tummy. Thump!

"Ha!" laughed somebody from the bank. "Bears can't skate!"

It was a hare with white fur, so white you could hardly see her against the snow. Her name was Frida.

"Then teach me," said Bruno, still lying on the ice.

And Frida did. Bruno learned to skate in the best way there is: by falling over. Sideways, backwards, spinning like a top with all four paws in the air.

That afternoon Tomás came along too, the fox with the enormous tail, to see what all the fuss was about. And that was how Bruno made his winter friends: the ones who don't go to sleep.

One afternoon, Bruno wandered further than ever, following some bird tracks.

And then up got the wind.

It wasn't the gentle air of the other days. This came hard, pushing the snow sideways, wiping out the paths, whistling through the pines.

Bruno walked and walked. But everything looked the same: white, white, white.

His paws were cold. His nose was frozen. And above all, he was enormously sleepy, so sleepy that his eyelids felt as heavy as two stones.

"I'll just close my eyes for a little while," he said.

And he sat down next to a fallen log, in the middle of the snow.

"Bruno! BRUNO!"

It was Frida and Tomás, up to their ears in snow. They had followed his stripy scarf, the only thing you could see in all that white.

"Up you get, bear!" said Frida. "You can't sleep here."

They pushed him and pulled him and took him between them to Tomás's den, under the roots of an oak tree.

It was small and dark, and as warm as a cup of milk.

Frida covered him with dry leaves. Tomás laid his enormous tail over Bruno's cold paws. Outside, the storm was still blowing. But inside, all you could hear was three friends breathing together.

"Thank you," said Bruno, his voice full of sleep.

"That's what winter friends are for," said Tomás. "To lend you their tail."

When the storm had passed, the forest was covered in sugar.

Bruno came out of the den and stretched. And he noticed something strange: everything felt heavy. His paws, his head, even his ears.

He sat down in the snow and thought for a while.

"I think my body is telling me something," he said slowly.

"What's it telling you?" asked Frida.

"That I've seen winter now. I've seen the snow, I've skated, I've made friends. And now it's time to sleep."

Frida gave him a hare hug, which is a very quick sort of hug. Tomás gave him a pine cone for the journey.

"Will you come back in spring?" he asked.

"I promise," said Bruno.

The way home was slow and lovely. Bruno left big round footprints in the snow.

Grandma didn't stir when he came into the cave.

Bruno took off his scarf and folded it carefully. He turned round three times on his bed of moss, the way bears do, and lay down snuggled up against Grandma.

He thought about the ice. About the bear with wings. About Tomás's tail.

He thought that winter was even lovelier than everyone had said.

And then, very slowly and very warmly, out came his first snore.

Outside, it was still snowing. Inside, a happy bear slept until spring.
